# Authorised testing: web, APIs and findings that get fixed

Run a small, authorised penetration test of the NimbuMart shop the way professionals do: rules of engagement first, recon inside scope, then three findings proved with the intercept proxy and the JWT inspector, scored with CVSS, written up so a developer can fix them, retested, and explained to the board.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `engagement.txt`, `findings.csv`, `net/dns.txt`, `net/hosts.txt`, `README.txt`, `staging-bundle.js.txt`, `wordlist.txt`.

## 1. Authorisation and scope, before anything else

A test without written permission is an attack. Read the letter of authorisation all the way through, then turn it into **rules of engagement**: who authorised it, exactly what is in and out of scope, the window, what you may and may not do, when you stop and who you call, and how you treat data.

```tool report
{"tpl": "roe", "title": "Rules of engagement: NimbuMart test, 16 to 20 November 2026", "text": "# Rules of engagement: NimbuMart test, 16 to 20 November 2026

## Parties and authorisation

NimbuMart Retail Pvt Ltd (client), represented by Ritu Malhotra, Head of Engineering, who signed the letter of authorisation on 12 November 2026. The tester works under that letter only.

## In scope

https://nimbu.shop and its /api; 192.0.2.10 shop-staging.nimbu.shop; 192.0.2.11 api-staging.nimbu.shop.

## Out of scope

192.0.2.12 pay.nimbu.shop (third-party payment provider); staff, phones and email; denial of service and load testing; changing or deleting other customers' data.

## Test window

Monday 16 November 09:00 to Friday 20 November 18:00 IST. No testing outside it.

## Allowed and forbidden techniques

Allowed: port and service scans of in-scope addresses, manual testing through an intercept proxy, offline checks of token secrets against a short wordlist. Forbidden: brute force against live logins, exploits that change data, anything against out-of-scope hosts.

## Stop conditions and contacts

Stop and call Ritu Malhotra (+91 98000 11223), or Dev Anand (+91 98000 44556), if live card data or real people's personal data appears, if something breaks, or if there are signs of a real attacker.

## Data handling

Use only the demo account. Read other customers' data only to prove a finding, one record at most. No copies leave the lab; screenshots cropped; working files deleted after the report.
", "n": 7, "blank": ["text"]}
```

- [ ] Every in-scope address and URL, and every out-of-scope one
- [ ] The stop contact and number, written where you'll see it
- [ ] What data you may touch, and how much

> Hint: A host can be on the same network and look like part of the shop and still be out of scope. Only the owner of a system can authorise testing it.

?> Which IP address is out of scope? :: sha256:a823b83a25d1af618351e48458d23bce176ddc6382e43243053d22f5cabffba6
?> Who is the stop contact? (full name) :: sha256:6ac6c3d112d73aaf6a5500393fcf57530d60d3e37d28f76ec71acce7d8e6347f

## 2. Recon, inside the lines

Scan only what's in scope. Name each address on the command line, so you can't accidentally sweep the whole range and hit the payment host. Then look at what you found.

- [ ] Which services run on each in-scope host, with which versions?
- [ ] Which one looks like it shouldn't be on the internet?
- [ ] What did you find in the staging JavaScript file?

> Hint: A "debug" API on port 8080 is a classic staging leftover. Read the saved app.bundle.js: developers leave things in bundles that everyone can download.

?> Which port does the staging debug API listen on? :: sha256:6c237681e70921603a306be9a1a5d9833fce5c1e268f52b1650970eaad0dce21

## 3. Finding 1: a login that trusts what you type

In the shop, the login puts the email straight into a SQL query inside quotes. End the quote and comment out the password check, and you're whoever you name. Prove it with **one** request in the web proxy, as admin, and stop there.

```tool proxy
{"m": "POST", "p": "/api/login", "h": "Content-Type: application/json", "b": "{\"email\": \"admin@nimbu.shop'--\", \"password\": \"x\"}", "s": 200, "blank": ["p", "b"]}
```

Then do the same in **Hack the shop** (mission "Log in as the admin"), and see the fix in the **SQL injection lab**: a parameterised query.

- [ ] The request, the response status and the role you got
- [ ] Why it works: the query the server built
- [ ] The fix, in one line a developer can follow
- [ ] The retest: the same request should now get 401

> Hint: `'--` closes the email's quote, and `--` starts a SQL comment, so `AND password = ...` is never checked.

?> Which HTTP status does the injected login get? :: sha256:27badc983df1780b60c2b3fa9d3a19a00e46aac798451f0febdca52920faaddf

## 4. Finding 2: someone else's order

Log in as the demo customer and open one of your orders. The API call is `/api/orders/` and a number. Change the number. If the shop gives you an order that isn't yours, that's an **insecure direct object reference** (IDOR): the API checks that you're logged in, not that the thing is yours.

```tool proxy
{"m": "GET", "p": "/api/orders/2", "h": "Authorization: Bearer {{token}}", "b": "", "s": 200, "blank": ["p", "b"]}
```

- [ ] Log in as demo@nimbu.shop first (Login tab), so `{{token}}` holds your token
- [ ] Your own orders are 3 and 4; ask for 2
- [ ] Note what you saw, then stop: one record proves it
- [ ] The fix: the query must include the caller's user ID

> Hint: Writing down someone's address in a report is itself a data leak. Say "order 2 belongs to another customer; it showed a delivery address", not the address.

?> Which order number belongs to someone else and proves the finding? :: sha256:d4735e3a265e16eee03f59718b9b5d03019c07d8b6c51f90da3a666eec13ab35

## 5. Finding 3: a token anyone can forge

The staging bundle holds a login token. A JWT is three parts: header, payload, signature. The signature only protects the token if its secret is hard to guess. Load the token in the JWT inspector, read what it says, and check its secret against the wordlist. That's an offline check: nothing is sent to the server.

```tool jwt
{"tok": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjMsImVtYWlsIjoiZGVtb0BuaW1idS5zaG9wIiwicm9sZSI6ImN1c3RvbWVyIiwiaWF0IjoxNzk0Nzg3MjAwLCJleHAiOjE3OTUzOTIwMDB9.Fzr9zEuwVnUnfgATCUbpvWEij5UTAph5ZiS5msv6EUM", "secret": "nimbu2026", "blank": ["secret"]}
```

- [ ] What's in the header and payload? Which algorithm?
- [ ] Is the secret in the wordlist? Which word?
- [ ] With the secret, what could an attacker change? (role: admin)
- [ ] Two fixes: a long random secret from a vault, and the token out of the bundle

> Hint: The shop's own mission "Forge a token" shows the other classic JWT mistake: a server that accepts `alg: none`.

?> Which signing algorithm does the token use? :: sha256:45e883897fdb361c6b08c0ffebadd157abe857e79964732890dc82505ff10c32
?> What is the token's secret? :: sha256:0c1fca450447b7ba7e29f162b714bcb817b86999ee0fc4124937ef35b6c98092

## 6. Score and rank

Score each finding's CVSS vector, then rank the register. CVSS describes the flaw; the ranking adds whether it's reachable from the internet and whether anyone is exploiting it.

```tool patch
{"vec": "CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H", "n": 9.8, "blank": ["vec"]}
```

- [ ] Score all three vectors
- [ ] Rank the register: which is first, and why?
- [ ] For NM-02, why is Privileges Required "Low"?

> Hint: The IDOR needs a customer account, which anyone can create for free. So PR:L is honest, but don't let it make the finding sound minor.

?> What is the CVSS base score of the login bypass? :: sha256:fd263f51d2398f2219b7f31c9c964dc7eff00b31bab1a7b7e59426fd52500de0

## 7. Write findings a developer can fix

A finding nobody can reproduce doesn't get fixed. For each one: the exact request, what came back, why it works, the fix in code terms, and the retest. Keep the data out: say what you saw, not the customer's address.

```tool report
{"tpl": "findings", "title": "Penetration test findings: NimbuMart, 16 to 20 November 2026", "text": "# Penetration test findings: NimbuMart, 16 to 20 November 2026

## Rules of engagement

As agreed in the letter of 12 November (see the rules of engagement): nimbu.shop and its /api, 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.11. 192.0.2.12 was not touched. Only the demo account was used.

## Executive summary

Three weaknesses let an outsider log in as the shop's administrator, read other customers' orders, and make the staging API believe they are anyone. All three are quick to fix. The first should be fixed before the weekend.

## Findings

**NM-01 Login bypass by SQL injection (critical, CVSS 9.8).** Reproduce: POST /api/login with `{"email":"admin@nimbu.shop'--","password":"x"}`; the response is 200 with role admin. Cause: the email is pasted into the SQL query. Fix: a parameterised query (`WHERE email = ? AND password = ?`). Retest: the same request returns 401.

**NM-02 Any customer can read any order (high in practice, CVSS 6.5).** Reproduce: log in as demo@nimbu.shop; GET /api/orders/2 returns another customer's order, including a delivery address. Cause: the query checks the order ID only. Fix: `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?` with the caller's ID from the token; return 404 otherwise. Retest: order 2 returns 404 for the demo account.

**NM-03 Staging tokens can be forged (critical, CVSS 9.1).** Reproduce: take DEMO_TOKEN from http://api-staging.nimbu.shop:8080/static/app.bundle.js; its HS256 secret is a dictionary word (checked offline against a 12-word list). Fix: a 32-byte random secret from the vault, rotated; remove the token from the bundle; put staging behind the VPN and close port 8080 to the internet. Retest: the old token is rejected; the secret isn't in any wordlist.

## What went well

Passwords are hashed; the payment page is separated and run by a provider; error messages on most pages don't show internals.

## Retest

Booked for Wednesday 25 November, same scope, same account.
", "n": 5, "blank": ["text"]}
```

- [ ] A developer could reproduce each finding from your text alone
- [ ] Each fix is specific (a query, a setting), not "improve security"
- [ ] Each has a retest
- [ ] "What went well" is honest: tests that only list failures get ignored

## 8. Retest, then tell the board

Retest each fix the same way you proved it: the same request should now fail. Then write the board note: no SQL, no CVSS, just what could have happened to the business, what it costs to fix, and what you need them to decide.

```tool report
{"tpl": "escalation", "title": "Note to the board: what the security test found", "text": "# Note to the board: what the security test found

## The ask

Please approve a one-week fix sprint starting Monday 23 November, and make a retest before any release a standing rule.

## Severity and why

High. Today, anyone on the internet could log in to the shop as its administrator, read other customers' orders, and impersonate any user on our test system.

## What we know

- The tester proved each problem with one request, using only a demo account; no customer data left the test.
- Each problem has a clear, small fix: about two days of developer time in total.

## What we don't know

- Whether anyone found these before us. The logs from before 16 November should be checked for the same requests.

## Impact so far

None known. If exploited: changed prices and orders, customers' addresses exposed (a personal data breach to report), and loss of trust in the shop.

## What I've done

Shared the findings with Engineering on 20 November; the login fix is already in testing.

## Evidence

The findings report and rules of engagement, 20 November 2026; retest booked for 25 November.
", "n": 7, "blank": ["text"]}
```

- [ ] The ask is the first line
- [ ] Impact in business words: money, customers, regulators
- [ ] What you don't know (has anyone else found these?)

> Hint: Boards decide on money, time and risk. "Two days of developer time to close three ways in" is a decision they can make.

## 9. Hand in

Hand in this notebook. It carries every answer, tool result and report from the steps above.

**Rubric**

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---|
| Rules of engagement complete before any test: authorisation, scope, window, stop contacts | 5 |
| Recon stayed inside scope, every command recorded | 3 |

- [ ] Rules of engagement written before testing
- [ ] Every command and request recorded
- [ ] Three findings with reproduction, fix and retest
- [ ] Board note written
- [ ] Press Hand in

script.intro: Welcome to Authorised testing. The word that matters is authorised: everything you do today is allowed because NimbuMart asked for it in writing, for these addresses, in this window, and nothing else. You'll write the rules of engagement before you touch anything, stay inside scope, prove three findings with as little data as possible, score them, write them so a developer can fix them, retest, and then explain to the board what it means for the business.
script.outro: That's a test that gets things fixed. Rules first, recon inside scope, three findings each proved with one request and no more data than needed, scored and ranked, written as steps a developer can follow, retested, and a board note in business words. Next is seminar ten: design, risk and audit, where you stop these problems before anyone has to test for them.
steps: A test without written permission is an attack, so we start with the letter. In scope: the shop, its API and two staging hosts. Out of scope: the payment host, even though it's on the same network, because NimbuMart doesn't own it. No social engineering, no denial of service, no touching other customers' data beyond proving a point. And the stop contact's number, written where we'll see it.

Recon, inside the lines. We name the two in-scope addresses rather than sweeping the range, so the payment host is never touched. Shop staging has SSH and the website. API staging has the API, and a debug API on port 8080 that shouldn't face the internet. Its JavaScript bundle contains a hard-coded token. Write every command down.

Finding one. The login pastes the email into SQL inside quotes. Close the quote, comment out the rest, and the password is never checked. One request in the proxy, status 200, role admin, and we stop. We don't browse the admin panel. The fix is a parameterised query, which the SQL injection lab shows, and the retest is the same request getting 401.

Finding two. Logged in as the demo customer, our orders are three and four. Ask for two, and the shop hands over another customer's order with a delivery address. The API checked we were logged in, not that the order was ours. One record proves it, and the report says it showed an address without writing the address down. The fix: the query includes the caller's user ID.

Finding three. The bundle's token is a JWT signed with HS256. The inspector decodes the header and payload: the demo customer, role customer. Then an offline check against twelve guessable words, and the secret falls out: nimbu twenty twenty-six. With that, anyone can sign a token that says role admin. The fix is a long random secret from a vault, and no token in a public file.

Scores. The login bypass is network, low complexity, no privileges, no user: 9.8, critical. The IDOR needs an account, but anyone can make one, so it's 6.5 and still serious. The token is 9.1. Ranked with exposure, the login bypass is first, then the token, then the orders.

A finding nobody can reproduce doesn't get fixed. Each one gets the exact request, what came back, why, the fix in code terms, and the retest. Not improve security, but where id equals this and user id equals that. And a section on what went well, because a report that only lists failures makes people defensive instead of busy.

Retest, then the board. Same requests, and now 401, 404, and a rejected token. The board note asks for a one-week fix sprint and a retest before every release, explains the risk as changed orders, exposed addresses and a breach to report, and says honestly what we don't know: whether anyone found these first.
Hand in the notebook: the rules of engagement, the recon commands, the three proofs, the scores, the findings report and the board note. The rubric is on screen.
